Relative income poverty is measured as a percentage of the population that earns less in comparison to [the median wage of the working population](Average_earnings "Average earnings").

In 2020 the [Australian Council of Social Service](Australian_Council_of_Social_Service "Australian Council of Social Service") released a report stating that relative poverty was growing in Australia, with an estimated 3.2  million people, or 13.6% of the population, living below an internationally accepted relative poverty threshold of 50% of a country's median income. Poverty lines can be set as either [absolute poverty](Absolute_poverty "Absolute poverty") lines or [relative](Relative_poverty "Relative poverty") poverty lines. Australia does not have an official poverty line, either absolute or relative. The ACOSS/UNSW report series entitled Poverty in Australia[[3]](Poverty_in_Australia#cite_note-PovertyAustraliaACOSS2012-3) uses two poverty lines and also took account of people's housing costs. One poverty line used by The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and in this study, referred to half of the middle income for all households, that is, 50% of median household income and the other is 60% of median income.[[3]](Poverty_in_Australia#cite_note-PovertyAustraliaACOSS2012-3)

It depends not only on income but also on access to services."[[6]](Poverty_in_Australia#cite_note-UN1995-6)
